articles.title: Fincantieri reports record backlog and raises 2026 earnings outlook
articles.summary: Italian shipbuilding group Fincantieri reported higher profitability in the first nine months of 2026, supported by stronger operating margins and continued demand across its main markets. articles.body: Italian shipbuilding group Fincantieri reported higher profitability in the first nine months of 2026, supported by stronger operating margins and continued demand across its main markets. The company also raised its full-year earnings guidance as its order backlog reached a new record. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) increased by 10.9% to €511 million, compared with €461 million a year earlier. Meanwhile, the EBITDA margin improved to 7.7%, up from 6.9% in the same period of 2025. However, revenue declined slightly to €6.61 billion from €6.73 billion last year. According to Fincantieri, growth in its commercial businesses and Underwater division partly offset changes in defence programmes and the impact of a major Indonesian naval order recorded in 2025. The company also strengthened its financial position. Adjusted net debt decreased to €730 million at the end of September, compared with €1.31 billion at the end of 2025. The improvement reflected cash generation and a capital increase completed in February. Shipbuilding backlog reaches record levels Fincantieri’s confirmed order backlog reached €44.7 billion, representing an 8.8% increase from the end of 2025. Its total backlog, including additional commercial commitments, rose by 14.9% to €72.6 billion. The company secured €9.7 billion in new orders during the first nine months of 2026. This represents approximately 88% of its annual order intake target of around €11 billion. In addition, Fincantieri signed contracts worth €12.3 billion that had not yet become effective by 30 September. These agreements were therefore excluded from the reported order intake. During the reporting period, the shipbuilder delivered 19 vessels from ten shipyards. Its order book included 90 vessels, with scheduled deliveries extending through 2036. The delivery horizon could extend to 2039 when including a Princess Cruises order signed in April 2026, which remains subject to financing. Fincantieri also highlighted a contract for two DDX destroyers for the Italian Navy. The agreement represents approximately €1.8 billion for the company, including €800 million in options. Revenue contributions are expected to begin as early as 2027. Fincantieri upgrades full-year guidance Following the improvement in profitability, Fincantieri increased its 2026 EBITDA forecast to between €715 million and €725 million. The previous guidance stood at €700 million to €710 million. The company maintained its full-year revenue target of approximately €9.3 billion to €9.4 billion. It also confirmed its expected net profit range of €140 million to €180 million. Meanwhile, Fincantieri revised its leverage outlook. The company now expects an adjusted net debt-to-EBITDA ratio of approximately 1.0, including the February capital increase, compared with its previous forecast of 1.3. “Our performance in the first nine months of 2026 confirms the acceleration in Fincantieri’s profitability, supported by structural demand across our reference markets and increasingly solid industrial and financial fundamentals,” said Pierroberto Folgiero, CEO and Managing Director, Fincantieri. Looking ahead, the company expects continued opportunities across naval defence, cruise ship construction and underwater technologies. Fincantieri is also expanding its industrial technology activities. Its recently announced partnership with Poste Italiane and TIM aims to develop an Italian physical AI value chain, combining advanced manufacturing capabilities with artificial intelligence.

The company also raised its full-year earnings guidance as its order backlog reached a new record.
Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) increased by 10.9% to €511 million, compared with €461 million a year earlier.

articles.title: DynaLiners Shares Index falls for fourth consecutive week
articles.summary: The DynaLiners Shares Index (DLSI) recorded its fourth consecutive weekly decline, falling by 111 points, or 4.1%, to 2,583, as losses spread across the maritime and container shipping sectors. According to DynaLiners, all sector indices finished the week lower, with the sharpest decline recorded by DLSI Carriers,...
articles.body: The DynaLiners Shares Index (DLSI) recorded its fourth consecutive weekly decline, falling by 111 points, or 4.1%, to 2,583, as losses spread across the maritime and container shipping sectors. According to DynaLiners, all sector indices finished the week lower, with the sharpest decline recorded by DLSI Carriers, which lost 239 points, equivalent to a 6% contraction. The latest figures extend a month-long downward trend in shipping-related equities, with container carriers experiencing particularly strong selling pressure. Declines outnumber gains across shipping stocks Negative performance was widespread among the companies tracked by the index, with 67 recording share-price declines compared with 53 that registered gains. The average share-price movement across the companies covered was a loss of 1.1%. Among the strongest performers, Vietnam’s An Giang Port led the gains with a 17% increase, closely followed by shipowner Seacon Shipping, whose shares advanced by 16%. Only one other company recorded an increase exceeding 10%. At the opposite end, Regional Container Lines (RCL) and Salalah Port registered the largest declines, with both companies losing 18% of their share value. Another six companies experienced share-price reductions of at least 10%, highlighting the extent of the downward pressure across the sector. The fourth consecutive weekly decline also raises questions about the divergence between investor sentiment and the earnings expectations of shipping companies. DynaLiners questioned whether carriers may have been too optimistic in their recent upward revisions to full-year expectations, particularly given the sustained weakness in shipping-related equities. However, stock market performance alone does not establish whether those financial projections will be achieved, with future earnings also dependent on freight market conditions, operating costs and developments in global trade.

articles.body: Interconnectors November 13, 2026 · 1 minute ago Orkney Islands’ first link to UK mainland nears offshore installation NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 1 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Nexans via LinkedIn Nexans has completed the factory acceptance test (FAT) of the 220 kV subsea cable that will connect the Orkney Islands to the UK mainland for the first time, in preparation for offshore installation that will start next year. The 220 MW Orkney Link, developed by SSEN Transmission, will comprise a new substation being built at Finstown, approximately 14 kilometers of underground cable installed across Orkney to Warebeth, and a 53-kilometer subsea cable laid to Caithness, where it will connect into a new substation at Dounreay. According to the company, the completion of the FAT testing represents the culmination of more than a year of manufacturing activities at its facility in Halden, Norway. "With this important manufacturing milestone achieved, project activities continue to progress on several fronts. Nexans' teams are currently advancing onshore cable installation and jointing works in Orkney, while preparations continue for the offshore installation campaign scheduled for 2027," Nexans said. Nexans started the installation of the underground land cable for the electricity interconnector this September. The installation will be done in phases, beginning in the east and progressing west towards Warebeth, where the cable will connect with the project’s future subsea section. articles.title: Seaway7 Starts Cable Installation at Ørsted’s Hornsea 3 Wind Farm
articles.summary: Seaway7 has installed the first inter-array cable at Ørsted's 2.9 GW Hornsea 3 offshore wind farm in the UK North Sea, marking the start of a major cable installation campaign.The company will transport and install more than 536 kilometers of 66kV inter-array cables…
articles.body: Seaway7 Starts Cable Installation at Ørsted’s Hornsea 3 Wind Farm Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 13, 2026 (Credit: Seaway7) Seaway7 has installed the first inter-array cable at Ørsted's 2.9 GW Hornsea 3 offshore wind farm in the UK North Sea, marking the start of a major cable installation campaign. The company will transport and install more than 536 kilometers of 66kV inter-array cables, connecting the wind turbines to offshore converter stations, Seaway7 announced on November 12. The scope covers 197 inter-array cables at Hornsea 3, which Seaway7 expects to become the world's largest offshore wind farm when completed. The project is the third in Ørsted's Hornsea offshore wind zone for which Seaway7 has secured an inter-array cable installation contract. The company previously transported and installed 89 cables totaling approximately 170 kilometers at Hornsea 1, followed by 165 cables spanning around 382 kilometers at Hornsea 2. Once the latest campaign is completed, Seaway7 will have installed more than 1,000 kilometers of inter-array cables across the three developments. The Hornsea projects are located approximately 90 - 160 kilometers off the east coast of England, in water depths ranging from around 25 to 75 meters. Delivery of the current installation program is being led from Seaway7's Aberdeen office.

articles.title: Singapore Retains Maritime City “Crown”, as Piraeus Jumps Up the Ranks
articles.summary: The maritime industry enters 2026 after another period of disruption and adjustment. Trade remains active, but the conditions supporting it have become more demanding. Geopolitical events are reshaping trade relationships and supply chains. Regional decarbonisation requirements are influencing operating costs and...
articles.body: Singapore Retains Maritime City “Crown”, as Piraeus Jumps Up the Ranks in International Shipping News 13/11/2026 The maritime industry enters 2026 after another period of disruption and adjustment. Trade remains active, but the conditions supporting it have become more demanding. Geopolitical events are reshaping trade relationships and supply chains. Regional decarbonisation requirements are influencing operating costs and investment decisions, and uncertainty remains over the timing and final design of a global greenhouse-gas framework. At the same time, digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence (AI) are becoming more deeply embedded in vessel, port and logistics operations. These developments are changing what maritime businesses require from the cities in which they operate. Strategic location and physical infrastructure remain essential, but companies increasingly emphasise access to specialist services, technology networks, capital and people with the right combination of maritime, digital, technical and commercial skills. The Leading Maritime Cities 2026 report assesses which cities provide the strongest environment for maritime companies and professionals to connect, operate and grow. The assessment combines objective data from leading international sources with the views of maritime experts from around the world. More than 15,000 cities were initially assessed using objective maritime indicators to identify 50 candidates for the final ranking. These cities were then benchmarked across five pillars: Shipping, Maritime Finance and Law, Maritime Technology, Ports and Logistics, and Attractiveness and Competitiveness. The 2026 assessment uses 48 objective and subjective indicators and incorporates responses from more than 200 maritime experts globally. Singapore remains the world’s leading maritime city in 2026. Shanghai rises to second place, followed by London in third, Rotterdam in fourth and Tokyo in fifth. Compared with the 2024 ranking, Singapore retains first place, while Shanghai moves up from fourth to second. London remains third, Rotterdam moves from second to fourth, and Tokyo enters the top five in place of Oslo. The results give Asia three of the top five cities, compared with two in 2024, reflecting the region’s strength across shipping, ports, shipbuilding, trade and maritime technology. Europe retains two positions in the top five through London and Rotterdam, whose highly developed maritime-service and port-industrial clusters continue to provide international influence well beyond their immediate regions. Singapore’s first-place position is built on exceptional breadth. It ranks first in Shipping, Ports and Logistics, and Attractiveness and Competitiveness, while also placing third in Maritime Finance and Law and fourth in Maritime Technology. The city combines large managed and owner-controlled fleets with a globally important port, strong liner connectivity, alternative bunkering capability and a wide range of maritime services. Experts also rank Singapore first as a shipping hub, technology hub, digitalised port, multi-fuel port and preferred location for maritime headquarters and research and development. Its leadership therefore does not depend on one activity. It reflects the way shipping, ports, finance, legal, technology, government and research institutions operate as a connected maritime cluster. Shanghai’s rise to second place reflects its strength across the physical and technological foundations of the maritime economy. It ranks first in Maritime Technology, second in Ports and Logistics and third in Shipping. The city combines the world’s largest container throughput and strongest liner connectivity with significant shipbuilding output, the highest number of maritime patents, and not least, a large and valuable fleet of ships. Its position within China’s manufacturing, cargo and industrial system creates close links between cargo demand, port activity, vessel ownership, shipbuilding and technology development. Shanghai’s performance shows how industrial scale can translate into wider maritime influence when several parts of the value chain are concentrated within the same hub. London retains third place through a very different maritime model. It ranks first in Maritime Finance and Law and third in Maritime Technology. The city remains the leading location for maritime legal expertise and marine insurance and is the preferred hub for maritime finance and dispute resolution. It also performs strongly in classification, engineering research, maritime technology start-ups, university programmes and human capital. London’s results demonstrate that a leading maritime city does not need to control the largest fleet or port. Its influence comes from the concentration of knowledge, capital, professional services and decision-making used by companies operating across the global maritime industry. Rotterdam ranks fourth overall and remains one of the world’s most complete port-industrial hubs. It places second in Attractiveness and Competitiveness and third in Ports and Logistics. Its strength extends beyond container handling to vessel traffic, energy, bulk cargoes, inland logistics and alternative-fuel infrastructure. Rotterdam also performs strongly in maritime technology start-ups, engineering research and expert assessments of resilience, digital-port capability and multi-fuel readiness. This diversified profile is increasingly valuable in an environment where ports must manage changing cargo flows while preparing infrastructure for new fuels, shore power and more integrated digital operations. Tokyo enters the overall top five through a broad base of established maritime and industrial capabilities. It ranks fourth in Shipping and performs strongly in fleet ownership, marine insurance, shipping-bank portfolios, maritime patents, classification and human capital. The city benefits from long-standing relationships between shipping companies, trading houses, banks, shipyards, equipment suppliers and research institutions. These connections provide a stable foundation for vessel investment and technical development, even though Tokyo receives less expert recognition than several more internationally oriented maritime-service hubs. Athens rises to 13th place globally, retaining its position as the world’s second-strongest shipping hub Athens records one of the most significant improvements in the global ranking of maritime cities, climbing from 35th place in 2024 to 13th in 2026. Its performance is even more impressive in the Shipping pillar, where it retains second place worldwide, behind only Singapore. The report by Menon Economics and DNV recognises Athens as the world’s leading shipowning hub, with the largest owner-controlled fleet and, by a considerable margin, the highest total fleet value. Specifically, the value of the Greek-controlled fleet attributed to Athens is estimated at approximately $203 billion, compared with around $90 billion for Tokyo. Athens is also home to 248 shipping companies operating more than five vessels, ranking second globally, behind Jakarta (337) and ahead of Singapore (219). Energy efficiency and the competitiveness of the Greek-owned fleet Athens also performs particularly well in indicators related to shipping’s energy transition. The city ranks third globally in the adoption of energy-saving technologies across its fleet, behind Taipei and Imabari. This is a particularly noteworthy achievement given the size and diversity of the Greek-owned fleet, as implementing energy-efficiency technologies across such a large and varied fleet presents considerable technical and operational challenges. In addition, Athens ranks second worldwide in the size of its owner-controlled fleet capable of using lower-carbon-intensive fuels, with approximately 3.3 million gross tonnes, compared with 5.1 million for Singapore. The report points out that this indicator reflects the fleet’s strategic flexibility rather than its actual emissions, since a vessel’s technical capability to use alternative fuels does not necessarily mean that those fuels are being used in practice. The individual pillar rankings show that maritime leadership can follow several paths. Athens remains the most powerful ownership hub and ranks second in Shipping, while Imabari enters the Shipping top five through its valuable owner-controlled fleet and strong adoption of energy-saving technologies. New York ranks second in Maritime Finance and Law through its listed maritime market and capital-raising activity. Busan ranks second in Maritime Technology and remains the leading shipbuilding hub, including for vessels capable of using lower-carbon-intensive fuels. Ningbo retains fourth place in Ports and Logistics through its container volumes, connectivity and exceptionally high vessel-call tonnage. Stockholm enters the Attractiveness and Competitiveness top five through strong innovation and institutional conditions, although its maritime-specific expert recognition remains more limited. The 2026 results also reflect a maritime energy transition moving from target-setting towards practical implementation. The proposed IMO Net-Zero Framework would combine a global fuel standard with a greenhouse-gas pricing mechanism, but discussions on formal adoption were adjourned in October 2025 and are scheduled to resume in December 2026. Owners, ports, financiers and fuel suppliers must therefore prepare for a lower-emission future while managing uncertainty over regulation, fuel availability and technology. The addition of new indicators covering fleet energy-efficiency adoption, shore power and wider port fuel capability gives greater visibility to cities that aim to be future-ready, helping the industry manage this uncertainty. Technology is creating a similarly broad shift. The Maritime Technology pillar now includes start-ups, engineering research and maritime university programmes alongside shipbuilding, classification and patents. The results distinguish between cities that produce technology and those that help bring it into operation. Shanghai and Busan lead industrial production, London leads several knowledge-based indicators, and Singapore receives the strongest expert recognition for technology, green transformation and research and development. This reflects a wider change in the maritime industry: the competitive advantage increasingly lies in connecting research, finance, testing, assurance and operational users rather than developing individual technologies in isolation. Across the five pillars, the strongest cities are those able to combine current maritime scale with the capability to adapt. They connect physical infrastructure with commercial decision-making, specialist services, technology and talent. They provide environments in which owners, operators, ports, financiers, technology companies, researchers and public institutions can work together. As trade, regulation and technology continue to evolve, this ability to coordinate across the maritime cluster will become an increasingly important source of competitiveness. Singapore leads because it brings these elements together more effectively than any other city, but the wider rankings show that maritime leadership remains internationally distributed across specialised and complementary hubs. articles.title: LAYUPMAN revision reaches key milestone in London
articles.summary: After months of online drafting sessions, BIMCO’s LAYUPMAN revision subcommittee met in person at the London offices of the International Transport Intermediaries Club (ITIC) for two days of intensive discussions, bringing the revised agreement closer to completion. LAYUPMAN, BIMCO’s standard agreement for the laying...
articles.body: LAYUPMAN revision reaches key milestone in London in International Shipping News 13/11/2026 After months of online drafting sessions, BIMCO’s LAYUPMAN revision subcommittee met in person at the London offices of the International Transport Intermediaries Club (ITIC) for two days of intensive discussions, bringing the revised agreement closer to completion. LAYUPMAN, BIMCO’s standard agreement for the laying up of ships, was published in 2011. The revision aims to provide a modern and flexible contractual framework capable of responding to different vessel types and layup arrangements. The London meeting tackled some of the most important issues in the revision, including the respective responsibilities of owners and layup managers, layup planning, deactivation and reactivation, insurance, liability, reporting and the scope of services during the layup period. The subcommittee also focused on ensuring that the agreement remains practical and adaptable rather than prescribing a single technical approach to laying up a vessel. The meeting also marked another chapter for majority of the subcommittee members who have worked together through a series of BIMCO ship management agreements, starting with SHIPMAN 2024, followed by CREWMAN A and B 2025, SUPERMAN 2025 and now the LAYUPMAN revision. This continuity has brought valuable practical experience and consistency to the development of BIMCO’s suite of ship management agreements. Bringing together a wealth of operational, technical and contractual expertise, the LAYUPMAN revision subcommittee is chaired by Ajay Hazari (formerly of Anglo Eastern) and comprises Juan J. Fernández-Ricoy (Naviera Elcano), Steve Davies (Anglo International Shipping Operations), Graham Prayel (V Ships), Manolis Nicolaou (Columbia Shipmanagement), Tim Howse (Gard P&I Club), Robert Hodge (ITIC) and Stephen Mackin (Hill Dickinson). “There is no one-size-fits-all approach to laying up a ship. Our aim with the revised LAYUPMAN has been to provide a clear contractual framework which has the flexibility necessary to accommodate different vessel types, locations and layup arrangements, taking into account the evolving requirements and practical realities of today’s maritime industry.” – Ajay Hazari, Chairperson of the LAYUPMAN Subcommittee With the London drafting meeting completed, the revised LAYUPMAN will soon be presented to the industry for consultation, giving stakeholders an opportunity to review and comment on the updated form before it moves through the final stages of BIMCO’s approval process. articles.body: IACS Publishes New Recommendation on Gas Dispersion Analysis (Rec.202) in International Shipping News 13/11/2026 IACS, the membership organisation for the world’s leading classification societies, has published a new Recommendation on gas dispersion analysis, marking a further significant contribution in its support of the safe decarbonisation of the maritime industry. The new guidance provides information on the best practices and requirements for carrying out gas dispersion analysis for Ships using gaseous fuels such as Ammonia and Hydrogen. Rec.202 is another significant deliverable from the IACS Safe Decarbonisation Panel and draws on several years of technical work and engagement with fuel manufacturers, technology providers, shipowners, shipbuilders, marine insurers and flag States. It provides a critical technical framework to support the safe use of alternative fuels such as ammonia and hydrogen, helping the maritime industry transition responsibly toward cleaner energy solutions. Recognising that the International Code of Safety for Ships Using Gases or Other Low-Flash-point Fuels (IGF Code) does not currently provide prescriptive requirements to address the hazards presented by alternative low or carbon-free alternative fuel options such as Ammonia, Hydrogen, etc., the IMO has developed interim guidelines for these fuels, including provisions for risk assessment and gas dispersion analysis. IACS’s Rec.202 supports this regulatory framework by providing detailed technical guidance for industry, IMO and other key stakeholders. Key highlights and benefits of Rec.202 include: Clear, Harmonized Best Practices for gas dispersion analysis The Guidelines establish harmonized best‑practice requirements for modelling flammability, toxicity, and gas‑dispersion hazards, ensuring a consistent and transparent basis for risk assessment across ship designs and fuel systems. By promoting a common technical understanding among IACS members, Flag Administrations, and industry stakeholders, they enhance confidence, support regulatory alignment, and enable the safe and effective deployment of alternative fuels Robust Expectations for Modelling Quality and Competency By specifying expectations for modeller competency, model validation, environmental conditions, and scenario selection, the guidelines strengthen the reliability and credibility of gas dispersion studies submitted to IACS members and Flag Administrations. Strengthening risk-based design and decision-making The Guidelines ensure that gas‑dispersion results are effectively integrated into ship design-informing decisions related to vent mast location, hazardous area classification, gas detection placement, ventilation design, and emergency planning, ultimately enhancing safety for crews and ships. Commenting on the publication of Rec.202, Robert Ashdown, the Secretary General of IACS said: “When IACS established its Safe Decarbonisation Panel in 2022, it explicitly recognised that some tasks would require joint working with flag States, industry bodies and others in order to deliver safe, responsible pathways for shipping’s decarbonisation, and a framework to facilitate such cooperation was devised. Rec.202 constitutes the first output arising from such a joint undertaking. It highlights how successful cooperation and coordination can result in outputs that advance the broader decarbonisation objectives of the industry and underpin other initiatives at IMO and elsewhere.” Source: IACS 2026-11-13 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: The new guidance provides information on the best practices and requirements for carrying out gas dispersion analysis for Ships using gaseous fuels such as Ammonia and Hydrogen.

It provides a critical technical framework to support the safe use of alternative fuels such as ammonia and hydrogen, helping the maritime industry transition responsibly toward cleaner energy solutions.

articles.body: Iran targets US radar in Bahrain, reports tanker explosion in Hormuz in International Shipping News 13/11/2026 Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Friday they had targeted a US early-warning radar in Bahrain, while the Guards’ navy reported that a liquefied natural gas tanker had struck a naval mine and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz, signalling continued risks to military assets and commercial shipping despite a fragile lull in the conflict. The Guards said the attack on the radar was carried out in retaliation for what they described as an air strike on a telecommunications tower in Sirik county, in Iran’s southern Hormozgan province, Iranian state media reported. The claim marks the first time since early September that Iran has said it attacked American military assets in a Gulf country. There was no immediate comment from Washington or Manama. The allegations came amid a tenuous pause in the conflict between Iran and the United States, which erupted after US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28 and subsequently spread across the region. Iran responded with missile and drone attacks on US bases in Gulf states and moves to restrict shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic passage for global oil and gas supplies. The United States imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports. In a separate statement, the Guards’ navy said the LNG tanker had struck a naval mine and suffered an explosion on Friday while navigating what it called an “unauthorised and dangerous route” through the strait. Iranian state media gave no further details about the vessel or its ownership. The report followed Iranian media accounts on Thursday that four oil tankers had been hit by explosions in the waterway. Those reports said the vessels had disregarded warnings and entered areas Tehran considers restricted. The incidents point to persistent dangers for shipping through Hormuz, even as vessel traffic has recovered and expectations of a de-escalation in the US-Israeli war on Iran have helped push oil prices lower. At least 10 ships came under attack in the first 10 days of November, following 37 attacks in October, the highest monthly total since the conflict began in late February, according to data from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. The latest claims underscore how the security risks extend beyond the direct confrontation between Iran and the United States, with commercial vessels continuing to face threats along one of the world’s most important energy corridors. articles.body: IMTRA Announces Leadership And Organizational Changes To Support Continued Growth in International Shipping News 13/11/2026 IMTRA, the leading manufacturer and importer of quality solutions and products for the marine, energy and transportation markets, announced today that Vice President of Recreational Sales Chip Farnham will retire after more than 40 years with the company. Alongside his retirement, IMTRA announced leadership and organizational changes designed to strengthen coordination across its sales, product management and operational functions and support continued growth. Farnham’s grandfather founded IMTRA, and his family held an ownership stake for 70 years. Throughout his career, Farnham has played an important role in IMTRA’s growth, building lasting relationships with customers and partners throughout the marine industry. In 2021, Farnham helped guide the decision to adopt an employee stock ownership plan (ESOP) to preserve IMTRA’s culture and transfer ownership to the employees who built the company and will carry it forward. His retirement marks the conclusion of more than four decades of service to the company and the boating community. He will continue to serve on IMTRA’s Board of Directors. “Chip has helped shape IMTRA into the company it is today, and his contributions extend well beyond sales,” said Eric Braitmayer, President and CEO, IMTRA. “The relationships he has built and the care he has shown for our customers have made a lasting difference to our business. We are deeply grateful for Chip’s more than 40 years of service and wish him the best in retirement.” As part of the transition, Alex Larsen, currently Vice President of Commercial Sales, has been named Executive Vice President. Larsen will oversee IMTRA’s recreational sales, commercial sales and product management teams, bringing these functions together under unified leadership. The structure is intended to encourage closer collaboration while preserving the specialized expertise and customer focus of each team. Reporting to Larsen, Christopher Barnes, Director of Recreational Sales, will lead the recreational sales team, while Eric MacDonald, Director of Commercial Sales, will lead commercial sales. Additionally reporting to Larsen, will be IMTRA Director of Product Management Colby Chevalier. Their market experience will support coordination with product management and help IMTRA respond to the distinct needs of its recreational and commercial customers. “These changes reflect our commitment to developing leaders from within and giving our teams the support they need to serve customers well,” added Braitmayer. “Alex, Christopher, Eric and Colby understand our business and the people who depend on us. Bringing their experience together in this structure will help us coordinate more effectively and build on the foundation Chip has helped establish.” Source: IMTRA 2026-11-13 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: CYTUR and PLAINBIT Sign MOU to Strengthen Maritime Cyber Incident Investigation and Response in International Shipping News 13/11/2026 CYTUR Inc. (CEO Yonghyun Jo), a maritime cybersecurity specialist, announced that it signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Plainbit Co., Ltd. (CEO Jinkook Kim), a company specializing in digital forensics and incident response, on November 11, 2026. The agreement aims to strengthen cyber incident investigation and response capabilities for vessels and maritime infrastructure. The partnership brings together CYTUR’s maritime-specific cybersecurity technologies and PLAINBIT’s expertise in Digital Forensics and Incident Response (DFIR) to establish a specialized framework for investigating and responding to cyber incidents in maritime environments. The two companies plan to develop a collaborative approach covering incident root cause analysis, digital evidence collection, incident response, and post-incident security improvements. Vessels and maritime infrastructure operate in complex environments where Operational Technology (OT), including navigation, machinery, and communication systems, is interconnected with Information Technology (IT). As a result, investigating and responding to maritime cyber incidents requires specialized expertise beyond conventional IT security. Effective incident investigations demand both an in-depth understanding of vessel systems and operational conditions and the ability to systematically collect, preserve, and analyze digital evidence. Under the agreement, the two companies will leverage their respective areas of expertise. CYTUR will focus on maritime cyber risk assessment and vessel OT security, supporting technical analysis for incident investigations using onboard asset information, security event data, and risk management records maintained through CYTUR-MG, its integrated cyber resilience management platform for vessels, and related systems. PLAINBIT will contribute its expertise in digital forensics and incident response, including digital evidence collection, preservation and analysis, root cause investigation, and compromise assessments of shipping companies’ shore-based IT environments. The collaboration aims to establish an incident investigation and response framework that addresses the unique operational characteristics of vessels while also considering interconnected shore-based IT systems. The two companies plan to jointly develop maritime-specific incident investigation procedures, digital evidence collection and preservation guidelines, and standardized investigation report templates. They will also explore incident response retainer services for shipping companies, joint incident response exercises and pilot projects involving operational vessels, collaborative research using anonymized incident cases and threat intelligence, and new business opportunities in domestic and international maritime markets. The partnership will also extend to maritime cyber insurance-related services. In October 2026, CYTUR signed an MOU with Hanwha General Insurance to collaborate on maritime cyber insurance initiatives. Building on this initiative, CYTUR and PLAINBIT plan to explore service models connecting pre-policy cyber risk assessments, compromise assessments during the insurance coverage period, and cyber insurance incident investigation and response. “As vessels and maritime infrastructure become increasingly digitalized and interconnected, specialized cyber incident investigation and response capabilities are becoming more important,” said Yonghyun Jo, CEO of CYTUR. “Through our collaboration with PLAINBIT, we aim to establish an incident investigation and response framework tailored to maritime environments and expand the foundation for services that enable shipowners and operators to better prepare for and respond to cyber threats.” Through this agreement, CYTUR and PLAINBIT will pursue the joint development of maritime-specific cyber incident investigation and response technologies and services, while expanding collaborative business opportunities across the global maritime industry, including shipping companies and shipyards. articles.summary: Germany remains one of the world’s most influential maritime nations. articles.body: Local knowledge, global reach: How LR is supporting Germany’s shipping industry in International Shipping News 13/11/2026 Germany remains one of the world’s most influential maritime nations. Home to leading shipowners, operators, ports, shipyards and equipment suppliers, it sits at the centre of many of the decisions shaping shipping’s future. Yet at a time when shipping is increasingly global and digital, one factor continues to matter: local expertise. Jens Grunenberg, Lloyd’s Register’s Germany Commercial Manager, discusses why local expertise remains critical in an increasingly global industry, how German maritime businesses are navigating rapid change, and why close relationships continue to matter when making complex technical and commercial decisions. Germany is home to globally connected shipping companies and access to expertise from around the world. Why does local presence still matter? What we have done is strengthen and scale up our German office. We are increasing our local presence while working within LR’s global network. That means German customers can access all of our global expertise, but delivered through people who they know and trust. In the heart of Hamburg, which is also central to Europe’s maritime industry, German customers have a German contact and the German office remains the main point of contact for them in all regards. Even though we have a global structure, the German office is still a key function and the first point of contact for any German client. We are close to the market. We are close to shipowners and managers. Sometimes we are only a mile away from major clients. We are not remote. We are there in person and can meet customers face to face. Our Hamburg office serves as far more than simply a regional outpost. We have all of our surveyors linked to the German office, whether they are operating in north-east Germany or north-west Germany. We have our machinery equipment department here in Hamburg, our account managers here and our new construction links here. Everything in regard to new construction goes via the Hamburg office. We have people focused on supporting German owners that may be building vessels in Asia or elsewhere in the world, which is quite normal today. We also have dedicated yard account managers and representatives responsible for German shipyards, such as Flensburger Schiffbau-Gesellschaft and other major yards.” We have strengthened those capabilities because German customers want to know there is somebody local who understands their business and can connect them into the wider global organisation when they need specialist support.” What are the biggest challenges German shipowners and operators are facing today? You can see it every day in the news. There is a lot of global friction at the moment. We see tensions in the Middle East, we see the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, and all of this is impacting and influencing the maritime industry. These pressures are driving costs, fuel costs in particular. Naturally, everyone wants to become more energy efficient. Everyone wants to reduce fuel consumption and reduce operating costs. Energy efficiency is definitely one of the biggest drivers we are seeing across the market. Regulatory pressure is also adding another layer of complexity. We have a lot of decarbonisation measures coming through. We are being required by IMO to reduce emissions and invest in new fuels that are more environmentally friendly. There are deadlines that need to be achieved, which means owners have to make important decisions now. Every new fuel means new safety regulations. Every new fuel means new approaches, additional work and more risk assessments. The way we have worked for many years is changing dramatically and it is changing very quickly. There are still a lot of question marks around what the right solutions are. Owners ask, ‘How can I achieve this? How can I manage this transition?’ If you are operating a large fleet, these are significant investment decisions that cannot be taken lightly. ‘’ LR’s strength is that we have three product portfolios. We are class, advisory and digital. Those three areas working together provide extremely strong support for our customers. ‘’ Jens Grunenberg, Germany Commercial Manager, LR Jens Grunenberg, Germany Commercial Manager, LR Why is local expertise especially important when helping customers navigate decarbonisation, digitalisation and energy efficiency? There is so much change happening at once. New regulations, new fuels, new technologies and new requirements are arriving much faster than we have ever seen before. When you are dealing with that level of change, you are looking for a local contact that you can talk to face to face. We are sitting right in the heart of Hamburg, which means we can easily have those face-to-face conversations with our customers, whether that is Hapag-Lloyd, Peter Döhle or many others across the German maritime community. While digital communication has become part of day-to-day business, I believe personal engagement remains critical. It is great that we can have Teams conversations and digital meetings, but walking into an office and speaking to someone face to face is still very different. German owners and managers really value that. Having German-speaking colleagues who understand the local culture and can communicate in the customer’s own language is a significant advantage. In such an international industry, that local connection and cultural understanding is something customers still highly appreciate. Being local to the companies and local to the clients is really a great asset. It helps build trust and makes it easier to support customers through difficult decisions. How do you help customers navigate uncertainty and make informed decisions? This journey can only be achieved as a team. Customers need colleagues, partners and joint approaches. Nobody can make this transition alone. LR’s strength is that we have three product portfolios. We are class, advisory and digital. Those three areas working together provide extremely strong support for our customers. From the advisory side we can carry out risk assessments, investigations and support business decisions. We can help an owner understand whether a future investment in a different fuel makes sense and what the implications might be. Alongside that, we have digital solutions that help improve energy efficiency, fleet performance, crew management and technical management. That means customers can access support across multiple areas through a single organisation. This joined-up approach is becoming a key differentiator. As a shipowner or manager, it is difficult to make this journey completely alone. There is always new technology, new regulation and new information emerging. Organisations naturally have limitations within their own teams. But we have the experience, we have the data and we have the expertise across class, advisory and digital. Bringing those three elements together allows us to support customers throughout the entire process. We can be connected to a vessel through digital solutions, support the owner through advisory services and provide classification expertise as well. That combination is unique. Looking ahead, why is Germany such an important maritime market? Germany has always been a very significant player in global shipping. We have major shipping companies, major ports, suppliers, technology providers and shipyards. We have companies like Hapag-Lloyd and Oldendorff. Hamburg is one of the largest ports in Europe. Bremerhaven is one of the largest car ports in Europe. For me, Germany’s importance extends beyond vessel ownership alone. When we talk about Germany as a maritime hub, we are not only talking about shipowners. We are talking about suppliers, equipment manufacturers, shipyards, logistics providers and ports. There is a very wide maritime ecosystem here. We have so many suppliers connected to the maritime industry and several ports that are crucial to global logistics. There is a lot happening around shipping in Germany, and that is what makes it such an important market. I believe local access will remain a critical part of serving that market. We are extremely close to our clients. They know where to find us. We can sit down together and discuss challenges directly. Customers can walk through the door and speak with us. In today’s world, personal relationships still matter. Being able to meet face to face, speak the same language and build trusted relationships remains a very strong asset. That breadth creates opportunities, but it also means businesses are managing change across an increasingly diverse and interconnected supply chain. articles.body: Ocean Network Express (ONE) has announced a reduction of approximately 18.2% in its Inland Fuel Charges (IFL/IFD) for carrier haulage operations in Thailand, effective from 20 November 2026. The revised charges will apply to import and export containers moving through Laem Chabang terminals via Bangkok Private Wharfs (BKK) and Lat Krabang (LKR), covering all trade lanes and transportation modes included in the carrier’s inland haulage arrangements. For shipments handled through Bangkok Private Wharfs, the surcharge on 20-foot containers will decrease from THB 330 to THB 270, while the charge for 40-foot containers will fall from THB 660 to THB 540. At Lat Krabang, the inland fuel charge will be reduced from THB 550 to THB 450 per unit. Revised inland fuel charges The updated charges, applicable to both import and export movements, are as follows: Location Previous charge New charge Bangkok – 20-foot THB 330 THB 270 Bangkok – 40-foot THB 660 THB 540 Lat Krabang – per unit THB 550 THB 450 The new rates will take effect on 20 November for both non-FMC-regulated trades and FMC-regulated trades, including shipments involving the United States and specified US territories, as well as Canada. The previous rates have been applicable since 23 October 2026. ONE introduced its inland fuel surcharge arrangements in Thailand earlier this year in response to fuel supply volatility and logistics challenges associated with developments in the Middle East. The carrier has linked the charges to disruptions in global fuel availability and distribution, including the impact of the security situation around the Strait of Hormuz. According to ONE, the surcharge is based on fuel costs and is subject to reviews and possible adjustments every two weeks. The revised charges will remain in effect until further notice, subject to applicable regulatory approvals and notification requirements. The latest adjustment reduces inland transportation costs for affected shipments, although ONE has not provided a specific explanation for the November reduction.

articles.summary: Dr Raymon Krishnan, president of Singapore’s Logistics & Supply Chain Management Society, writes for Splash today, reflecting on one of this week’s most talked about stories in the mainstream press. articles.body: Containers Contributions From ocean liner to artificial reef: A warning for container shipping Splash November 13, 2026 0 0 3 minutes read Dr Raymon Krishnan, president of Singapore’s Logistics & Supply Chain Management Society, writes for Splash today, reflecting on one of this week’s most talked about stories in the mainstream press. On Wednesday, the 990-foot ocean liner SS United States was deliberately sunk off Destin, Florida, to become what is expected to be the world’s largest artificial reef. Initial underwater inspections found the vessel upright, approximately 180 feet below the surface. The sinking of the SS United States reminds us that ships can outlive their commercial purpose. Launched in 1951 and entering service in 1952, the SS United States was the pinnacle of post-war American maritime engineering. It held the record as the world’s fastest passenger ship but was withdrawn in 1969 as commercial aviation transformed the economics of transatlantic travel. It was not poor engineering that made the ship obsolete, it was a market that had moved on. After decades moored in Philadelphia, the vessel was acquired by Okaloosa County in a project valued at approximately $13m. Its new role will support tourism, marine conservation and research. Its retirement offers a useful perspective on container shipping as it now faces another turning point. A substantial wave of new capacity The container shipping industry is preparing for a significant increase in fleet capacity. According to Drewry’s third-quarter 2026 Container Forecaster the global containership orderbook stood at approximately 13.9m teu on 1 September 2026, equivalent to 40.9% of the active fleet. Drewry forecasts fleet growth of 8.4% in 2027, rising to 12.1% in 2028 before moderating to 9.4% in 2029. The concern is the market into which these ships will be delivered. During the pandemic, congestion, equipment shortages and route disruption absorbed vessel capacity. Diversions around the Cape of Good Hope lengthened voyages and tied up ships. Carriers responded by ordering larger, more fuel-efficient vessels anticipating continued trade growth, but shipbuilding schedules are long and in the era of the never normal, market conditions change quickly. If Red Sea and Suez Canal routings return progressively to normal, shorter voyages could release significant effective capacity without a single additional ship entering service. Combined with newbuildings, this could widen the gap between supply and demand. Vessel capacity could potentially reach as much as 10% above demand under such circumstances. The consequences could include lower freight rates, tougher competition for cargo, blank sailings, slower steaming, vessel idling and accelerated recycling of older tonnage. The industry faces a major capacity-management challenge. The cost of getting the timing wrong Aviation permanently changed the market for passenger liners, while container shipping remains essential to trade. New vessels will not automatically become redundant. Nevertheless, ships are long-term capital investments, ordered years before delivery and expected to earn returns over operating lives spanning decades. A vessel ordered when freight rates are high and capacity constrained may enter service when demand is weaker, transit times are shorter and competing tonnage is plentiful. Efficiency alone cannot guarantee a satisfactory return. Carriers will have to decide which vessels to deploy, which trades to prioritise and when to redeploy or retire older ships. Smaller vessels displaced from mainline routes may move into regional trades, adding competitive pressure whilst others may be laid up, sold or recycled. Ports and terminals may see service patterns, berth requirements and transhipment flows change. Shippers may welcome lower rates but carriers protecting utilisation may consolidate services, withdraw sailings or alter port rotations. Lower prices could therefore come with less predictable frequency and transit times. The costs of poor capacity planning will ultimately ripple through businesses to end users and consumers. A different future for ageing vessels The SS United States project raises the question of what happens when ships lose their original commercial purpose. Conversion into an artificial reef offers a potential tourism and conservation role but it is neither a universal nor necessarily economical solution for commercial vessels. For surplus container ships, recycling will remain the principal end-of-life option when redeployment is no longer viable. Some older vessels may serve feeder networks or specialised trades, provided their economics remain competitive. Fleet renewal should consider the economic, environmental and operational consequences of retiring existing tonnage and not just the efficiency gains promised by newbuildings. The SS United States was a remarkable engineering achievement but it could not escape changing transportation economics. Its story reminds us that a ship’s commercial lifespan is determined not simply by how well it is built but by whether the market still needs what it does. As the industry approaches 2027, the question is whether carriers have ordered more capacity than the market can sustainably absorb and how prepared they are to manage the consequences. The challenge is not simply to build the next generation of vessels. It is to ensure there is a commercially sustainable reason to put them to work. It’s not something we as an industry have a good track doing. articles.body: A.P. Moller–Maersk has opened a new integrated logistics facility in Montevideo, Uruguay, following a private investment of more than US$20 million, expanding its container handling, storage and cargo services near the Port of Montevideo. The 71,000-square-metre facility is located along the Route 1 access corridor, at the intersection of Camino Cibils and Camino Burghi. It brings together container equipment services, cargo handling and inland logistics operations in a single location, with the aim of improving connectivity between the port and regional supply chains. The development provides storage capacity for 7,000 TEU, more than 1,000 pallet positions, 140 reefer plugs and 3,200 square metres of covered cargo handling and storage space. Its infrastructure also includes six inbound and six outbound gates, container-handling equipment and terminal tractors. New facility strengthens port connectivity The logistics platform combines empty-container storage, inspection, maintenance and repair with cargo services such as container stuffing and de-stuffing, cargo inspection, full-container storage and refrigerated container power supply. According to Maersk, consolidating these activities at one site is intended to reduce operational handoffs and improve flexibility for cargo moving between inland facilities and the Port of Montevideo. The facility will support both bonded and domestic operations, alongside integrated logistics management and value-added services. “Uruguay plays an important role in connecting regional supply chains with international markets. This investment strengthens our capabilities in Montevideo and our connection with the Port of Montevideo, while expanding the solutions we can offer customers moving cargo through the region,” said Antonio Dominguez, President for Latin America and the Caribbean at Maersk. The facility was inaugurated in the presence of Uruguay’s President Yamandú Orsi, senior government officials and Maersk executives. Energy efficiency and sustainability features The new logistics centre incorporates infrastructure designed to improve energy efficiency and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. The project is expected to achieve LEED Gold certification and includes solar panels for renewable electricity generation, automated temperature and climate-control systems, and humidity management technology. Its design also incorporates architectural features intended to maximise natural light and improve energy performance. Ricardo Rocha, President for the East Coast of South America at Maersk, said the integration of container services, cargo handling and storage would help connect inland operations more efficiently with the port and international markets. The investment expands Maersk’s logistics infrastructure in Uruguay as the company continues developing integrated transport and supply chain services across Latin America.

articles.body: Asia Gas BW LPG scores another lucrative Avance VLGC flip Adis Ajdin November 13, 2026 0 41 1 minute read Geir Vinnes / Marine Traffic Geir Vinnes / Marine Traffic BW LPG has struck another lucrative vessel sale, offloading a VLGC acquired in John Fredriksen’s Avance Gas fleet deal less than two years ago for well over $100m. The New York- and Oslo-listed gas carrier giant has agreed to sell the 2015-built, 83,134 cu m BW Mistral , with the transaction expected to generate a net book gain of around $37m and net cash proceeds of approximately $104m. Built at China’s Jiangnan shipyard, the scrubber-fitted vessel is currently trading in the spot market and will continue earning revenue for BW LPG until its scheduled handover by mid-January 2027. The disposal marks another profitable exit from the 12-ship Avance Gas fleet acquired in August 2024 for $1.05bn in cash, shares and assumed debt. In July, BW LPG agreed to sell the 2015-built, 83,000 cu m BW Levant , another vessel from the Avance transaction, with expected net cash proceeds of $38m and a book gain of around $17m. The two deals are set to generate combined book gains of approximately $54m and net cash proceeds of $142m. The latest sale comes amid a broader fleet renewal drive at BW LPG. Its 52%-owned Indian subsidiary has also been selling older VLGCs, most recently agreeing to dispose of the 2008-built BW Loyalty for a price in the low-$80m range, with an expected gain of $52m. At the other end of the fleet, BW LPG has committed around $940m to eight 90,000 cu m panamax VLGC newbuildings at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in South Korea, scheduled for delivery between 2029 and 2030. The Mark Young-led company said it had conditionally allocated 108.5m shares at NOK17.44 ($1.83) apiece, taking up the full $25m over-allotment on top of its original $175m fundraising target. The transaction comprises 95m new shares raising approximately $174m for Cetus, alongside 13.5m existing shares borrowed from major shareholder Pacific Transportation Asia (PTA) to cover the over-allotment. A 30-day greenshoe option could bring in further capital through the issuance of additional new shares. Together with DNB Asset Management, the four investors had indicated interest in subscribing for a combined $106.5m. Cetus has not disclosed their final individual allocations. The proceeds should help fund Cetus’s acquisition of 13 handysize and ultramax bulkers from Hong Kong-listed Seacon Shipping Group, along with Syngrace, which holds contracts for three additional handysize newbuildings. The transaction involves approximately $72.5m in cash and the issuance of 37.3m Cetus shares to Seacon. The fresh capital will also support newbuilding payments, fleet deleveraging and working capital requirements. Following completion of the fleet acquisition and a planned vessel sale, Cetus said it expects to operate 42 ships, comprising 34 vessels on the water and eight newbuildings scheduled for delivery in 2027 and 2028. The company is targeting November 18 for its first day of trading on Euronext Growth Oslo, subject to regulatory approvals and completion of the Seacon transaction. The measures also cover nine companies, including Russian oil producer Slavneft, Rosneft’s Vostok Oil project and several energy trading businesses based in Dubai. The latest vessel additions include LNG carriers Melicertes, Neleus, Perle, Aeolus and Oneiroi , alongside the Novatek-linked Koryak FSU . On the oil side, London has blacklisted Apeks, Sara Sky, Balu 6, Yvika and Alma . The vessels operate under a mix of Russian, Panamanian, Sierra Leonean and Djiboutian flags, according to the official sanctions notice. The restrictions prohibit the specified ships from accessing British ports and impose controls on chartering and operating them. They also restrict the provision of services including ship finance, broking, technical assistance and crewing, subject to applicable exceptions and licensing arrangements. The corporate additions extend the crackdown beyond individual ships. Dubai-based Forteza Trading, Patera and Novus Energy have been designated, with British authorities specifically linking Novus Energy to dealings involving vessels already subject to UK restrictions. Russian petrochemical producer Sibur and coal groups SUEK and Kuzbassrazrezugol also feature in the latest package. The move brings all ten of Russia’s largest oil producers under British sanctions following the inclusion of Slavneft. The government announced the measures during the European Political Community summit in Dublin, where pressure on Russian energy revenues formed part of discussions on Ukraine. Britain has been steadily expanding its maritime restrictions this year, including sanctions against six ships in August and an earlier package targeting Russia’s developing LNG shadow fleet. Preparations for the transition are already underway, including technical and operational handover, workforce integration and the transfer of operating processes and systems. The contract adds to Deutsche Windtechnik’s growing offshore wind maintenance portfolio. articles.body: The Port of Los Angeles handled 1,026,872 TEUs in October 2026, setting a new record for the month. The figure also represents the second-highest monthly container volume in the port’s history. For the first time, the port exceeded 1 million TEUs in two consecutive months. The October performance followed September’s all-time record of 1,042,652 TEUs, marking another milestone for the busiest container port in the United States. The port has now surpassed 1 million TEUs three times in 2026. Furthermore, container throughput between June and October reached nearly 5 million TEUs, the strongest five-month period in its history. Port of Los Angeles Executive Director Gene Seroka attributed the sustained activity to consumer spending, inventory replenishment and changes in trade policy. Ongoing disruptions along other global shipping routes have also influenced cargo movements. According to Seroka, the port’s ability to manage consistently high volumes reflects the coordination between terminal operators, shipping lines and other supply chain partners. Imports increase as empty container volumes reach new record Loaded imports reached 538,620 TEUs in October, representing a 25% increase compared with the same month last year. Import volumes were also 30% above the port’s five-year October average. However, loaded exports declined by 7% year-on-year to 114,981 TEUs, highlighting the different trends in inbound and outbound cargo flows. Meanwhile, empty container movements reached 373,271 TEUs, setting another monthly record. This marked the second consecutive month of record empty container volumes as shipping lines repositioned equipment to Asia for future shipments. The strong October performance lifted total container throughput for the first ten months of 2026 to 9,108,497 TEUs. This represents a 5% increase compared with the same period in 2025 and places volumes 9% above the five-year average. The figures also underline the port’s strong performance during the second half of the year, despite continued uncertainty surrounding international trade and shipping routes. Port prepares for 2028 Olympic Games During the monthly cargo briefing, Seroka was joined by Reynold Hoover, CEO of LA28, the organising committee for the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games. The discussion focused on preparations for the event, including the port’s role as the Olympic sailing venue and planned improvements along the LA Waterfront. The two organisations are coordinating preparations to accommodate the event while maintaining commercial port operations. The Port of Los Angeles remains the leading container gateway in the United States. It handled approximately 10.2 million TEUs in 2025 and has ranked as the country’s busiest container port for 26 consecutive years.

articles.summary: Greenpeace has identified 540 possible oil spills across the Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Arabian Sea since the US-Iran war began on February 28 (see map below), with satellite imagery showing a cumulative slick footprint of approximately 20,000 sq km. Not all detections have been conclusively linked to attacks on...
articles.body: Environment Middle East Tankers Gulf war leaves toxic legacy that could last decades Sam Chambers November 13, 2026 0 342 2 minutes read CENTCOM CENTCOM Greenpeace has identified 540 possible oil spills across the Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Arabian Sea since the US-Iran war began on February 28 (see map below), with satellite imagery showing a cumulative slick footprint of approximately 20,000 sq km. Not all detections have been conclusively linked to attacks on shipping. The environmental consequences could last for decades. A 2022 study published in the Journal of Marine Science and Engineering found extensive oil deposits along more than 25 km of Saudi Arabia’s Abu Ali Island coastline, almost 40 years after the 1983–85 Nowruz oil spills during the Iran-Iraq war. Researchers found oil contamination in 76% of 1,434 test pits, demonstrating how petroleum residues can persist long after surface slicks disappear. The spills continue daily with many more strikes on ships being reported every week. Iran has claimed that four oil tankers struck naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz over the past two days, while a separately confirmed attack on a Sinokor-operated tanker off the United Arab Emirates forced the evacuation of 22 seafarers. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy claimed yesterday that two supertankers carrying more than 4m barrels of oil between them had been disabled by explosions on Wednesday after ignoring warnings against using what Tehran described as an unauthorised route through the strait. Iranian state media attributed the explosions to naval mines and broadcast footage purporting to show the incidents. The Iranian army subsequently claimed that another two tankers struck mines in the eastern part of the strait on Thursday afternoon after ignoring navigation warnings and switching off their radar systems. None of the four vessels has been identified, and the claims have not been independently verified. Separately, UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) confirmed that a tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile 14 nautical miles northwest of Ras Al Khaimah, UAE, at 1800 GMT on Wednesday. The projectile hit the vessel’s engine room, starting a fire and forcing the evacuation of its crew. India’s shipping minister Sarbananda Sonowal subsequently identified the vessel as the Liberia-flagged Dominica Prosperity, reporting that all 22 crew members, including 19 Indian nationals, had been safely evacuated. articles.title: Baltic Exchange and Mercuria await verdict in landmark tanker index trial
articles.summary: One of shipping’s most consequential legal battles has concluded in London, with the Baltic Exchange and commodities trader Mercuria awaiting a High Court ruling on whether the industry’s leading VLCC freight benchmark should have continued operating after war erupted in the Middle East. The three-week trial ended...
articles.body: Europe Tankers Baltic Exchange and Mercuria await verdict in landmark tanker index trial Sam Chambers November 13, 2026 0 325 2 minutes read One of shipping’s most consequential legal battles has concluded in London, with the Baltic Exchange and commodities trader Mercuria awaiting a High Court ruling on whether the industry’s leading VLCC freight benchmark should have continued operating after war erupted in the Middle East. The three-week trial ended yesterday, with judgment expected to take several months. At the centre of the dispute is TD3C, the Baltic’s benchmark for transporting crude from Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia to Ningbo, China, a voyage requiring passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Mercuria has argued that the disruption following the outbreak of hostilities on February 28 rendered the benchmark unreliable, with insufficient physical tanker activity to support meaningful assessments. The trading house maintains that the Baltic failed to meet its statutory and contractual obligations by continuing to publish rates despite mounting evidence that its contributing shipbrokers could not reliably determine a market price. During the trial, Mercuria highlighted internal communications revealing considerable uncertainty among Baltic staff and broker panellists. One Baltic assessor reportedly described the rates as “utter nonsense”, while a contributing broker questioned how a market could be assessed when virtually no vessels were fixing voyages. Mercuria also challenged the Baltic’s reliance on forward freight agreement prices when calculating a benchmark that itself underpins derivatives contracts, raising concerns about circular pricing. However, the trader significantly narrowed its case during closing arguments, abandoning demands for retrospective invalidation or suspension of the index. The Baltic, owned by the Singapore Exchange, has vigorously rejected the allegations, arguing that its established methodology remained appropriate despite extraordinary market conditions. Its lawyers maintain that experienced shipbrokers could still assess freight values using available market intelligence, including transactions, vessel movements and derivatives pricing. The exchange also pointed to continuing vessel transits through Hormuz during the disputed period, disputing Mercuria’s contention that there was no meaningful underlying market. In closing arguments, the Baltic accused Mercuria of repeatedly changing its case and suggested the litigation was an attempt to escape the consequences of unsuccessful trading positions. Mercuria rejected allegations of wrongdoing. The Baltic has also warned that retrospective intervention in a widely used benchmark could create significant uncertainty for freight derivatives and physical shipping contracts linked to TD3C. The dispute has exposed uncomfortable questions about the governance of shipping’s freight indices, particularly when geopolitical events make conventional market assessments exceptionally difficult. The Baltic Exchange has consistently defended its benchmark procedures and regulatory compliance. Mr Justice Andrew Baker must now determine whether those procedures satisfied the exchange’s obligations during an unprecedented disruption to tanker trading. The implications extend well beyond the two companies, potentially influencing how freight benchmarks are maintained during future market emergencies. articles.title: Port of Helsingborg to introduce Secure Container Release for import containers
articles.summary: The Port of Helsingborg is preparing to introduce Secure Container Release (SCR), a digital system designed to strengthen security and traceability in the release and pickup of loaded import containers. Developed by Antwerp-based technology provider T-Mining, the system will link container pickup rights to verified...
articles.body: The Port of Helsingborg is preparing to introduce Secure Container Release (SCR), a digital system designed to strengthen security and traceability in the release and pickup of loaded import containers. Developed by Antwerp-based technology provider T-Mining, the system will link container pickup rights to verified driver identities, with full implementation scheduled for 31 March 2027. The Swedish port has partnered with T-Mining to introduce SCR across its loaded import container operations. As Sweden’s second-largest container port, Helsingborg handles approximately 400 container pickups each day. The initiative builds on earlier security investments, including a dedicated customs facility and Sweden’s first permanent cargo scanner. SCR is intended to address security risks associated with traditional container release procedures, particularly the sharing of manual release references across logistics chains. Under the new process, ocean carriers will issue container releases digitally, with pickup rights transferred securely through freight forwarders and transport companies to designated drivers. The solution forms part of wider industry efforts to standardise secure container release procedures. Through the Digital Container Shipping Association’s (DCSA) DCSA+ programme, SCR is working with shipping lines, ports and terminals to promote standards-based digital container releases. “Security is a shared responsibility across the entire logistics chain. At Port of Helsingborg, we continuously work to strengthen both physical and digital security, while making our processes more efficient for our customers. With SCR, we add another important layer of protection to the container release process. The close dialogue our commercial department is having with the shipping lines is key to making the transition secure and smooth for everyone involved,” said Joakim Sandberg, CSO at Port of Helsingborg. Digital verification at the terminal gate Under the planned system, freight forwarders will receive container release rights digitally and transfer them securely to transport companies. The transport company will then assign the pickup right to an identified truck driver, establishing a traceable chain of authorisation from the shipping line to the person collecting the container. At the terminal’s automated gate, the driver’s identity and pickup authorisation will be checked against the digital container release before the container is handed over. The process is designed to reduce reliance on manually shared release information and limit opportunities for unauthorised container collection. Phased implementation scheduled for March 2027 The Port of Helsingborg will introduce SCR in phases ahead of its full launch on 31 March 2027. Shipping lines operating at the port are being introduced to the new process in advance, while freight forwarders, transport companies and other stakeholders will receive information and onboarding support ahead of implementation. T-Mining said its Secure Container Release solution has already been used to manage more than five million container handovers since 2016, with deployments involving shipping lines and terminals internationally. “Since 2016, we’ve implemented Secure Container Release with leading carriers and terminals around the world, securing the handover of more than 5 million containers. We’re proud to partner with the Port of Helsingborg to ensure the secure release of loaded import containers at the port,” said Nico Wauters, CEO at T-Mining. The SCR platform is already deployed at European ports including Antwerp-Bruges and Rotterdam. According to T-Mining, its network connects more than 8,000 logistics companies across over 25 countries. The Port of Helsingborg handles approximately 270,000 TEU by sea and 60,000 TEU by rail annually, serving shipping lines, freight forwarders and transport operators through its road, rail and maritime connections.
