articles.title: New report identifies Hong Kong’s place in world shipping
articles.summary: Hong Kong Maritime Week is about to kick off. To celebrate the occasion, Splash today publishes a 48-page magazine on the city’s maritime hub credentials. A ship can be ordered at a mainland Chinese yard, owned through a leasing company in Hong Kong, insured in London, crewed through a management operation in Asia...
articles.body: Contributions Greater China New report identifies Hong Kong’s place in world shipping Splash November 13, 2026 0 933 8 minutes read Hong Kong Maritime Week is about to kick off. To celebrate the occasion, Splash today publishes a 48-page magazine on the city’s maritime hub credentials. A ship can be ordered at a mainland Chinese yard, owned through a leasing company in Hong Kong, insured in London, crewed through a management operation in Asia and chartered from Singapore. Its cargo need never pass through Hong Kong’s harbour. Even its Hong Kong financing vehicle may have to seek credit approval elsewhere. The geography of shipping has always been complicated. What has changed is the urgency with which Hong Kong must ask where the real business takes place. Is the city still a maritime capital in its own right, chosen by international owners, traders and financiers because of what it offers? Or is it becoming a highly sophisticated services counter for the vast industrial and commercial machine next door? On paper, the answer looks reassuring. Hong Kong remains fourth in the 2026 Xinhua-Baltic international maritime centre rankings, behind Singapore, Shanghai and London. Three of the world’s leading shipmanagement companies are headquartered here, major P&I clubs operate here, and the city retains a formidable concentration of lawyers, financiers and technical expertise. Look towards the waterfront, however, and a different picture emerges. The container port handled 12.99m teu in 2025, scarcely half its 2008 peak. The register has shed substantial tonnage amid geopolitical upheaval, falling to 109m gt by June this year. Shanghai, Shenzhen and Guangzhou have grown into maritime giants whose physical advantages Hong Kong cannot realistically overturn. These are not contradictory stories. Together they define the central question running through this special report: whether Hong Kong can convert its inherited maritime strengths into a sustainable business model for 2030, even as its traditional measures of importance become less flattering. Richard Hext, chairman of the Hong Kong Shipowners Association, resists the suggestion that the city is being reduced to an adjunct of the mainland. “An ‘annex’ does not host three of the world’s top 10 shipmanagers, 11 of the 12 International Group P&I associations, eight of the top ten ship-finance bookrunners,” he says, pointing also to the city’s legal institutions and international industry organisations. This inventory represents decades of investment and commercial trust. Yet it does not settle the more difficult question of what those institutions actually do here, or whether their next expansion will take place somewhere else. Where the decisions are made Hong Kong has spent much of this decade making itself more attractive on tax. Qualifying ship lessors can enjoy a zero profits-tax rate; eligible ship leasing managers, shipmanagers, agents and brokers benefit from half-rate treatment, as do certain marine insurers. The administration has also sought to broaden the proposition to physical commodity traders, recognising that traders create demand for chartering, insurance, finance and legal services The first results are tangible, but open to interpretation. Government figures show the number of ship leasing enterprises under the relevant preferential regime rising from 11 in 2020/21 to 46 in 2022/23. That is evidence that structures and businesses have responded. It says much less about the location of credit committees, the people selecting vessels or the teams negotiating charters. “Tax is necessary but not sufficient,” Hext says. Companies, he argues, follow customers, skills, capital and regulatory certainty. He wants the next phase judged by “regional headquarters, underwriting authority, credit decisions, trading desks and skilled jobs, and not by company registrations alone”. Gautam Chellaram, chairman of KC Maritime, is more sceptical about what tax reform has delivered. He sees genuine growth in leasing and mainland-linked finance, but says: “I do not yet see clear evidence that the measures have resulted in substantial headquarters relocation involving decision-makers, fund managers, and independent shipowners physically basing themselves in Hong Kong.” It would be equally wrong to dismiss the developments as bookkeeping. Hong Kong is a place where ships are managed, risks assessed and capital arranged, not merely where documents are signed. Dockendale Group is among the companies expanding management operations locally. Its chief executive, Vikrant Gusain, says Hong Kong’s ease of doing business is an important factor in the decision, alongside access to Asian markets and international talent. The competitive comparison nevertheless remains Singapore. “Singapore continues to offer broader tax incentives and a larger concentration of commodity traders,” says Jim James, senior consultant at Hill Dickinson. The latter point may be more important than the former. Traders and charterers bring transactions, and transactions bring the brokers, lenders, insurers and lawyers who serve them. A critical mass of principals is extraordinarily difficult to manufacture through concessions alone. Hong Kong has distinct advantages of its own. Its banking network connects Chinese and international capital; its offshore renminbi role creates opportunities for trade and leasing; and its links with a vast manufacturing and shipbuilding hinterland provide access that a competing maritime centre cannot reproduce. But geographical proximity is not the same thing as commercial gravity. The city must persuade companies to put people with mandates and budgets here, not just a local subsidiary. June’s tax amendment bill, including a proposed half-rate concession for qualifying physical commodity trading, gives the policy another push. September’s first five-year plan adds a ‘Finance + Maritime’ agenda built around ship finance, insurance, trade finance and related services. Neither initiative can be called successful solely because it exists. Their test will be new trading desks, lending decisions and customers with genuine freedom to transact elsewhere. The mainland advantage — and the danger Where does this leave the argument that Hong Kong is becoming Shanghai’s professional-services annex? Chellaram offers the report’s most uncomfortable formulation: as a cargo port, the city is being functionally subordinated to mainland competitors, but as a financial, legal and arbitration centre it retains qualities not available in the same combination across the border. “On the professional-services side, Hong Kong is the piece Shanghai structurally cannot replicate,” he says. The separate customs territory, common-law system, freely convertible currency and established international business practices all give the city a distinctive purpose. The opportunity is to sell those qualities to the world, not simply to companies moving through China. Damien Laracy, partner and head of Hill Dickinson’s Hong Kong office, describes a transition “from a cargo-driven port hub to a specialised centre for maritime services”. Rather than an annex, he sees “the region’s high-value maritime services platform, complementing the manufacturing, cargo, and port capacity of neighbouring cities”. The distinction is subtle but critical. A law firm advising a mainland shipowner on a vessel financing can be doing genuine international business from Hong Kong. So can an insurer handling a casualty thousands of miles away or a manager overseeing a fleet trading between Brazil and India. But the city’s position becomes more vulnerable if its principal attraction is merely that it makes mainland transactions easier. The international test is whether owners and counterparties with no direct mainland connection still choose Hong Kong. The machinery of a genuine maritime centre is already here. English-language maritime contracts, established common-law precedents, internationally recognised arbitration and access to mainland enforcement arrangements give it a credible offering. Rosita Lau, a partner at Ince, is among those urging the city to promote its legal and dispute-resolution capabilities far more systematically. The fact that Hong Kong can be chosen in a contract is not proof that it will be. There are also more prosaic measures of legal competitiveness. Martyn Huckerby, head of competition law and regulatory at Hill Dickinson, points to the extension of the block exemption for liner vessel-sharing agreements to 2031. The renewal, he says, preserves “legal certainty for operational cooperation between liner shipping companies”. It is a narrow regulatory decision, but one of the many predictable rules on which internationally mobile businesses build long-term operations. Insurance offers another illustration of integration without inevitable subordination. London P&I has served shipowners from Hong Kong for decades and opened an office in Shanghai in 2025. Deborah Yu, its regional director for Asia, says the two offices work together with the club’s operations in London and Athens. The point is not to force every Asian insurance decision into Hong Kong, but to ensure the city continues to handle work that could plausibly be located elsewhere. International outlook An international city must keep choosing to be international. That means foreign owners can operate comfortably, specialist staff can build careers and global counterparties can trust their contracts, information and capital to an environment they understand. This issue explores what that requirement means in practice. Hong Kong’s shipmanagement concentration provides a genuine strategic asset: it would take years to reproduce the crewing, technical and training networks that leading managers have built here. The challenge is keeping enough experienced people to make decisions locally as digitalisation, alternative fuels and increasingly complex compliance change the skill set. The same logic applies to finance and insurance. An internationally recognised logo on a Hong Kong office does not tell us whether it can approve a ship loan or underwrite a specialist risk. A registry’s gross tonnage does not establish where the family that owns the ship runs its business. A port’s box count says little about the value of transactions governed by local law, but the loss of container activity cannot be waved away simply by relabelling the city a services centre. Technology adds a further test. Hong Kong’s Port Community System is meant to help connect cargo movements, documentation and financing across the supply chain. But common platforms are only as useful as the trust and security behind them. Paul Haswell, technology partner at Hill Dickinson, notes that digitisation will bring “increased emphasis on data security and the monitoring of systems”. A financial and logistics crossroads cannot afford to treat cyber resilience as an optional extra. The city’s new maritime ambitions, particularly green bunkering and transition finance, depend on the same mixture of hard infrastructure and intangible trust. There is little value in promoting alternative fuels unless ships can take them safely, on schedule and at competitive prices. There is little point marketing green ship finance unless lenders and owners are prepared to commit capital against realistic assumptions about technology, fuel availability and earnings. Government has clearly recognised the need to change. Its first five-year plan shifts the emphasis from volume to value, promising stronger maritime services, a greener and smarter port, closer links with the Greater Bay Area and a more developed marine finance ecosystem. The question is no longer whether officials have ambitions. It is whether businesses can see projects proceeding quickly enough, and with sufficient commercial substance, to justify staying and expanding. That demands a sharper understanding of competition. Singapore can be a partner and a rival. Shanghai can be a customer, collaborator and competitor. The Greater Bay Area can supply Hong Kong with enormous commercial opportunities while simultaneously taking cargo, talent and investment from it. Those apparently inconsistent propositions are the reality of a maritime industry in which business moves wherever the overall proposition is strongest. The defensible future is neither a nostalgic campaign to win back every container nor a comfortable acceptance of being the mainland’s legal and financial back office. It is a city that remains indispensable to international shipping because substantive work is done there: ships are managed, cargo is traded, capital is committed, risks are insured and disputes are resolved. By 2030, Hong Kong should be judged less by how many companies have an address in Central or how many development plans have been published, and more by who has authority to do business from the city. Are the next fleet acquisitions decided here? Are traders locating profitable operations here? Are international parties choosing Hong Kong law when they have no obligation to do so? Are young maritime professionals staying because the best opportunities are available here? A gateway is somewhere business passes through. A maritime capital is somewhere business chooses to stay. Hong Kong has spent generations proving it can be both. The coming four years will show whether it still can. You can read the magazine ahead of Hong Kong Maritime Week by clicking here . articles.body: Asian Terminals has secured a 25-year renewal of its concession to operate and develop Manila South Harbour. The renewed agreement, signed with the Philippine Ports Authority, will run from May 2038 to May 2063, giving long-term certainty for the continued development and modernisation of one of the country’s key international trade gateways. The renewal comes in ATI’s 40th anniversary year. Over those four decades ATI has invested more than PHP 42 billion in developing and modernising its Philippine port facilities. Its operations have moved approximately 30 million TEUs of containers, 57 million metric tonnes of non-containerised cargo and 70 million passengers. The next phase will focus on future-proofing Manila South Harbour against changing trade patterns, rising cargo volumes and the evolving needs of shipping lines, importers, exporters and the wider logistics community. Plans include capacity expansion, greener and more energy-efficient cargo-handling equipment, greater automation and advanced digital technologies, aimed at delivering safer, smarter and more sustainable end-to-end port and logistics solutions. Essa Kazim, Executive Chairman of DP World, said the Philippines has significant long-term growth potential and that the renewal provides the certainty needed to plan and invest for decades ahead, reflecting DP World’s belief in the country’s economic future. Jason Varsamidis, CEO and Managing Director of DP World Asia Pacific, described the renewal as a strong endorsement of ATI’s track record and its partnership with the Philippine Ports Authority, and said the focus now turns to investment in capacity, technology and more sustainable operations to keep the terminal competitive, efficient and responsive to customers.

Join the leading maritime news network Image courtesy SS United States: An Operational Guide to America's Flagship The SS United States has settled upright on the floor of the Gulf of Mexico, completing its transformation from record-breaking ocean liner to the world’s largest artificial reef. Early sonar and remotely operated vehicle inspections confirmed that the 990-foot vessel came to rest upright, just feet from its intended location, following its controlled sinking off Florida’s Gulf Coast on Wednesday, November 11. The first underwater images are also emerging. RV Explorer, a shipwreck research and salvage vessel based in Cape May, New Jersey, shared an image of diver Captain Will Hinton positioned in front of the ship’s stern. “Happy to report the SS United States is sitting perfectly upright,” RV Explorer said. The confirmation marks a significant milestone for a project that required extensive preparation to ensure the historic vessel would settle safely on the seabed and remain accessible to divers. According to Destin-Fort Walton Beach tourism officials, the ship now rests approximately 22 nautical miles offshore in about 180 feet of water, with its uppermost deck roughly 60 feet below the surface. The safety zone surrounding the deployment site has been lifted, allowing divers to begin exploring the wreck. “The successful deployment of the SS United States is a significant achievement, and I couldn’t be prouder of the team,” said Jennifer Adams, tourism director for Destin-Fort Walton Beach. “To see a vessel of this size come to rest upright, within feet of its intended location, is a great testament to the expertise and collaboration of everyone who helped bring this ambitious vision to life.” The SS United States was deliberately sunk on Veterans Day after weather concerns prompted Okaloosa County to move the operation forward from its original November 12 schedule. Hundreds of spectators gathered aboard nearby boats to witness the final moments of the ship that once held the title of the world’s fastest ocean liner. Crews opened intake valves to allow Gulf waters to flood the vessel in a controlled sinking operation. The ship gradually submerged before rolling to port and sinking below the surface, eventually settling onto the seabed. The deployment followed extensive work to prepare the former passenger liner for its new role, including environmental remediation and structural modifications designed to make the wreck safer for divers and marine life. The SS United States joins more than 580 artificial reef sites in the Destin-Fort Walton Beach area, although none comes close to matching its scale. “This sets Okaloosa County apart as a leader in the tourism industry worldwide and we could not be happier to see this project come to fruition,” said Okaloosa County Board Chairman Trey Goodwin. Beyond its significance as a diving attraction, the ship will become a large-scale marine research site. Scientists from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, Dauphin Island Sea Lab and Louisiana State University will monitor biological, physical and chemical changes around the vessel as marine organisms begin colonizing its structure. Researchers hope the project will provide new insights into how artificial reefs develop over time and support marine ecosystems. “This is so much more than creating a new dive destination,” said Alex Fogg, natural resources chief for Destin-Fort Walton Beach. “It’s an opportunity to advance marine science on a scale we’ve never experienced before.” For the SS United States , the deployment marks another chapter in a remarkable history. Built in Newport News, Virginia, the liner entered service in 1952 and set a transatlantic speed record on her maiden voyage that remains unbeaten by any ocean liner. After retiring in 1969, she spent decades laid up, including a long period on the Philadelphia waterfront, as preservation efforts struggled to secure her future. Now, the former flagship has a permanent home beneath the Gulf. A future shoreside museum and visitor experience, being developed with the SS United States Conservancy, will preserve the ship’s history and artifacts for visitors who may never venture underwater. “Her legacy will live on,” said Conservancy Board Chair Susan Gibbs. The artificial reef project was funded through tourism revenue and contributions from project partners. articles.summary: By Lori-Ann LaRocco The Port of Los Angeles handled a record 1,026,872 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in October, marking its second-busiest month ever and extending the strongest five-month cargo run...

By Lori-Ann LaRocco The Port of Los Angeles handled a record 1,026,872 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in October, marking its second-busiest month ever and extending the strongest five-month cargo run in the port’s 118-year history. The October total followed September’s all-time record of 1,042,652 TEUs, marking the first time the nation’s busiest container port has surpassed 1 million units in consecutive months. Los Angeles has now crossed that threshold three times in 2026, another first. “On the heels of September’s all-time record, October makes it our second-best month ever,” said Port Executive Director Gene Seroka during a media briefing. “No other U.S. port has handled 1 million units in a single month, and we’ve now done it three times this year, including back-to-back months for the first time ever.” From June through October, the port processed nearly 5 million TEUs, its strongest five-month stretch on record. “What’s remarkable isn’t just the record volume but our ability to sustain this level of activity month after month,” Seroka said in a statement Thursday. Seroka attributed the historic cargo activity to continued consumer spending, retailers replenishing inventories, changes in trade policy and disruptions along other global shipping routes. Loaded imports reached 538,620 TEUs in October, up 25% from a year earlier and 30% above the port’s five-year October average. “This strength goes beyond holiday merchandise,” Seroka said. “We’re moving consumer goods alongside parts, components, and equipment destined for American businesses and manufacturers across the country.” The port also handled a record 373,271 empty TEUs, surpassing the previous monthly record set in September. Ocean carriers have been repositioning equipment to Asia to accommodate additional shipments. Exports, however, remain a weak spot. Loaded exports totaled 114,981 TEUs, down 7% from October 2025. “Exports have now declined year over year in six of the first 10 months here in 2026, as American farmers and manufacturers continue to face headwinds in overseas markets,” Seroka said. Through October, Los Angeles has handled 9,108,497 TEUs, 5% ahead of last year and 9% above its five-year average. Seroka said November volumes are also shaping up to be strong, raising the possibility of another annual record. “If December also delivers, I believe this could be the busiest year in our port’s 118-year history,” he said. Despite the historic volumes, a potential labor disruption and mounting rail delays threaten to complicate cargo movements at the neighboring ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. The Pacific Maritime Association and International Longshore and Warehouse Union Local 26, which represents about 250 maritime watchmen at the ports, have extended contract negotiations through November 20 . The extension temporarily averts a walkout, but a strike remains possible if the two sides fail to reach an agreement. Although the watchmen represent a small portion of the waterfront workforce, a work stoppage could have a much broader impact. Other ILWU locals, including longshore workers in Local 13 and marine clerks in Local 63, have indicated they would honor Local 26 picket lines. A strike would come as both ports are already struggling with elevated intermodal container dwell times. Recent port data showed approximately 9,500 rail-bound import containers at Los Angeles had been waiting nine days or longer for on-dock rail transportation. At Long Beach, another 5,063 containers faced similar delays. Separate import dwell-time data from Los Angeles showed approximately 67% of containers moving through terminals within four days, while 11% remained five to eight days and 23% stayed nine days or longer. Logistics provider C.H. Robinson has identified a shortage of intermodal railcars in Southern California as a contributing factor to the slowdown. Trucking capacity is also under pressure. “Port congestion at LA and Long Beach due to increased import volume and reduced driver capacity continues to be highly elevated,” said Paul Brashier, vice president of global supply chain at ITS Logistics. “With congestion reducing the amount of containers a driver can execute daily, shippers should be prepared to add additional trucking capacity to navigate these conditions through Lunar New Year.” Any labor disruption could further extend container dwell times and create additional challenges for importers moving goods inland. Despite the operational pressures, Seroka remains optimistic about cargo demand heading into next year. After two visits to China and discussions with manufacturers, he said factories there are running at full capacity, with exporters anticipating strong shipments through the end of 2026 and into early 2027. The temporary easing of U.S.-China tariff tensions has provided some relief for shippers, while the extension of the suspension of U.S. port fees targeting Chinese vessels has removed another near-term source of uncertainty. Importers are also expected to accelerate shipments ahead of Lunar New Year, contributing to the elevated cargo flows. Still, the outlook remains vulnerable to further changes in trade policy, including potential Section 301 tariffs, the direction of U.S.-China negotiations and renewed tensions surrounding advanced semiconductor technology. There are also questions about how long American consumers can sustain the current pace of spending. High energy and food prices continue to pressure household budgets, while rising consumer debt raises additional questions about demand heading into 2027. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York recently reported that U.S. credit card balances reached a record $1.29 trillion in the third quarter. Another source of cargo demand—and uncertainty—is the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure. Trade data provider ImportGenius has been tracking shipments of data center components and infrastructure moving through Los Angeles and Long Beach as technology companies expand their computing capacity across the United States. But questions about future projects, electricity availability and the political environment could influence how much equipment continues to move through the ports. “The big players in the AI space have been competing largely on the capabilities of their models,” said Lynn Hughes, lead analyst for the trade research team at ImportGenius. “Recent election results and limited grid capacity will cause investors in data centers to re-evaluate their exposure. But it’s very likely that the next area of competition is efficiency in training and inference.” For now, the Port of Los Angeles is closing out 2026 with record cargo momentum and the prospect of its busiest year ever. Whether that pace can continue into 2027 will depend not only on consumer demand and U.S.-China trade relations, but also on the ability of Southern California’s ports, railroads and trucking networks to keep freight moving. Saronic has awarded a contract worth more than $100 million to Norway’s Syncrolift to design and supply what the companies say will be the world’s largest shiplift at its planned $3 billion Port Alpha shipyard in Brownsville, Texas. The system will feature a 300-meter (984-foot) lifting platform with a capacity of 67,000 metric tons, more than twice the lifting capacity of the next-largest installation, according to Saronic’s announcement Thursday. Syncrolift, a subsidiary of Oslo-listed Nekkar ASA, will manage the project from its headquarters near Oslo. The company previously disclosed the contract on November 4 without identifying the customer, calling it the largest order in its history. Final delivery is scheduled for 2028. The massive shiplift will play a central role in Saronic’s plans to rethink how ships are built, allowing multiple vessels to be assembled and outfitted simultaneously on land rather than occupying traditional dry docks. Instead of building ships in fixed docks, Port Alpha is being designed around a production system in which large hull sections are assembled and vessels move between workstations. The shiplift and accompanying transfer system will allow completed ships to be moved from their construction positions into the water. The tandem lifting system will incorporate condition-monitoring technology and digital-twin controls to monitor operations throughout the lifting process. “The scope and scale of this shiplift is foundational to how the yard will operate,” said Doug Lambert, Saronic’s co-founder and chief operating officer. The approach is intended to reduce bottlenecks associated with traditional shipbuilding, where dock availability and limited waterfront space can constrain production. By moving more construction and outfitting work onto land, Saronic aims to increase the number of vessels that can be built simultaneously. The contract marks another major step in the development of Port Alpha, which broke ground on September 30 . Located at the Port of Brownsville, the shipyard will initially occupy 835 acres, with the potential to expand to nearly 4,400 acres. Saronic plans to invest more than $3 billion in the project, which it says could eventually support up to 10,000 direct jobs. The facility is being developed to build both autonomous and crewed vessels for commercial and defense customers, reflecting growing efforts to expand U.S. shipbuilding capacity amid concerns over the country’s declining share of global ship production. According to Saronic’s Port Alpha development plans , the initial phase will accommodate ships measuring up to approximately 850 feet, with future expansion potentially supporting vessels exceeding 1,200 feet. The company is targeting initial operations in 2028, with plans to eventually produce as many as 20 ships annually by 2035. Its first vessels are expected to be Landing Craft Utility vessels under a U.S. Navy contract. Saronic is also working with South Korea’s Samsung Heavy Industries as it develops its shipbuilding capabilities. The Syncrolift agreement highlights the role international suppliers are expected to play in the project, even as Saronic positions Port Alpha as a major investment in rebuilding domestic maritime manufacturing capacity. The contract was announced in connection with the Atlantic Future Forum, a gathering of defense, security and technology leaders focused on cooperation among allied nations. articles.title: Finland Detects Strike on Baltic Sea Russian Warship
articles.summary: Finland's military said on Thursday its forces had detected "a strike" on a Russian warship in the Baltic Sea a day earlier, but that the security situation in the area remained stable.It was not immediately clear if there were any casualties or what had caused the strike.
articles.body: Finland Detects Strike on Baltic Sea Russian Warship Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 12, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Flavijus Piliponis Finland's military said on Thursday its forces had detected "a strike" on a Russian warship in the Baltic Sea a day earlier, but that the security situation in the area remained stable. It was not immediately clear if there were any casualties or what had caused the strike. Estonian media reported on Thursday that the vessel was a small Russian navy ship and that it later returned to St Petersburg. "The Finnish Defence Forces detected... a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland area and has monitored the development of the situation," a spokesperson for the Nordic country's military said in an emailed statement to Reuters. Finland is not under any immediate military threat, the spokesperson added. The defence forces declined to provide further details about the location or timing of the incident, or how it was detected. Ukraine has been sending waves of military drones towards Russia's northwest Leningrad region, which includes the city of St Petersburg as well as the Baltic Sea port of Ust-Luga, a major export outlet for commodities such as oil and grain. Some Ukrainian drones have strayed into the airspace of Finland and the Baltic region, leading to fears that the war is spilling over into NATO countries that border Russia and its ally Belarus. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania early on Wednesday issued warnings to citizens to take shelter due to drones in their airspace, and NATO scrambled warplanes in response. The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia that extends eastwards to St Petersburg. (Reuters)

articles.summary: Oil prices rose on Thursday by more than $1 a barrel, as continued disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and broader geopolitical tensions offset pressure from rising crude output that had sent prices lower in early trade.Brent…
articles.body: Oil Prices Rise $1/Barrel As Disruptions Continue in Strait of Hormuz Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 12, 2026 © Adobe Stock/PX Media Oil prices rose on Thursday by more than $1 a barrel, as continued disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and broader geopolitical tensions offset pressure from rising crude output that had sent prices lower in early trade. Brent futures were up $1.2 or 1.3% a barrel at $93.96 at 12:08 p.m. ET or 1508 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate crude was up 53 cents or 0.6% at $87.06. Both benchmarks were still headed for a weekly decline. Prices fell early, and had been trading steady to lower before President Donald Trump wrote on social media that the US did not need a deal with Iran. "Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!" he wrote. In the strait, tankers are still ablaze, oil spills are washing ashore and drones and missiles have hit infrastructure across the region. On Thursday, Iran's military said four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz after ignoring warnings. Reuters could not immediately verify the Iranian accounts. Attacks on shipping in the Middle East have increased in recent weeks. The Strait of Hormuz carried nearly one-fifth of the world's crude oil before the US-Israel conflict with Iran. Elsewhere, Ukraine continued attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, saying it targeted the port area of Ust-Luga by the Baltic Sea in Russia's northwest with drone attacks which triggered a fire and damaged part of its network of fuel tanks. Ust-Luga is a major oil, oil products and grain export outlet, along with other commodities. "The tit-for-tat exchanges between Russia and Ukraine and attacks on shipping by the IRGC are beginning to add additional price pressure," said Timothy Snyder, chief economist at Matador Economics. "It is beginning to look like investors are growing weary from hearing the same song on peace prospects." OPEC PRODUCTION RISES OPEC+ crude production rose in October, driven by higher Saudi Arabian output despite shipping disruptions through the strait. Ukraine peace talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner began in the Kremlin. In a potential breakthrough, a US envoy said Putin agreed to include European representatives in the next round of negotiations. In the US, crude stocks, gasoline and distillate inventories rose last week, the Energy Information Administration said on Thursday. Washington is set to extend a waiver to a US law in coming days allowing some foreign-flagged ships to transport oil and other commodities between US ports, four industry sources said on Thursday. (Reuters)

articles.title: White House to Extend Jones Act Shipping Waiver
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's administration is set to extend a waiver to a US law in coming days allowing some foreign-flagged ships to transport oil and other commodities between US ports, four industry sources said on Thursday.The extension will…
articles.body: White House to Extend Jones Act Shipping Waiver Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 12, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Vacclav President Donald Trump's administration is set to extend a waiver to a US law in coming days allowing some foreign-flagged ships to transport oil and other commodities between US ports, four industry sources said on Thursday. The extension will require individual voyages to undergo case-by-case review rather than allowing foreign ships to receive blanket exemptions from the Jones Act, two sources said. The waiver is one of the tools the administration has used to try to lower diesel and gasoline prices, which have been driven higher by the wars in Iran in Ukraine. The waiver could come as early as Thursday, one of the sources said. The administration last extended the waiver in August until November 15, and it has already been the longest waiver in history for the more than 100-year old law. A White House official said no decision has yet been made on the extension of the Jones Act waiver, adding that any announcements will be made directly Trump or his administration. The Jones Act requires cargo moving between US ports to be carried on ships built in the US, owned by US companies and crewed by American workers, and the waiver aims to lower gas prices by increasing shipping flexibility and reducing transport ‌bottlenecks. While the Jones Act waiver increases the availability of tankers to move fuel, it ⁠would likely only reduce gasoline prices by pennies per gallon, some analysts and industry experts have said. About 300 waivers were provided under the blanket Jones Act waivers in March and May, while about 48 waivers have been provided under the exemptions from August, which had limited the scope of the waivers, data from the administration showed. US gasoline prices averaged about $3.91 on Thursday, compared with $2.98 before the US-Iran war, while diesel prices have risen to $6.10 versus $3.76 before the war, according to data from AAA. (Reuters)

articles.title: Four Oil Tankers Struck by Hormuz Explosions
articles.summary: Four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's military said on Thursday, adding that the vessels had ignored warnings and entered what it considers restricted areas of the strategic waterway.Tankers are still facing attacks across the strait…
articles.body: Four Oil Tankers Struck by Hormuz Explosions Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 12, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Noor Afzal Four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's military said on Thursday, adding that the vessels had ignored warnings and entered what it considers restricted areas of the strategic waterway. Tankers are still facing attacks across the strait, despite a rebound in traffic and expectations of a de-escalation in the war between the United States and Iran that have been reflected in falling oil prices. Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said two supertankers were disabled by explosions on Wednesday after they ignored warnings against using what it said was an "unauthorised route". Reuters could not immediately verify the Iranian account. The two vessels "exploded after hitting naval mines", Iranian state media reported, broadcasting what it said was video footage of the incidents. Iran's army later said two other tankers had hit mines on Thursday afternoon while sailing through the eastern Strait of Hormuz after ignoring warnings and disabling their radar systems, state TV reported. The tankers entered a restricted area and subsequently caught fire, it reported. Earlier in the US-Israeli war with Iran, which began in February, the IRGC Navy announced its attacks on tankers. More recently, however, it has instead reported that vessels have caught fire after hitting naval mines while traversing the southern part of the strait, which it has declared an unauthorised route. In several of those cases, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO) has said vessels had been struck by unknown projectiles. The UKMTO said in reports on Thursday that a vessel was hit by an unidentified projectile about 14 nautical miles northwest of the UAE emirate of Ras Al-Khaimah on Wednesday while exiting the strait, causing a fire in its engine room. Firefighting efforts were under way and all crew had been evacuated, it added. At least 10 ships were hit in the first 10 days of November, after 37 attacks in October, which was the highest monthly tally since the conflict began in late February, according to data from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. (Reuters)

REUTERS/Stringer A projectile struck the engine room of the Liberia-flagged crude oil tanker Dominica Prosperity off the United Arab Emirates on Wednesday, forcing the evacuation of all 22 crew members as emergency crews battled a fire aboard the vessel. The attack was one of four tanker incidents documented in the latest maritime security advisory covering the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, including a separate strike that left multiple seafarers injured. According to UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), the Dominica Prosperity was struck by an unidentified projectile at approximately 1800 UTC on November 11, about 14 nautical miles northwest of Ras Al Khaimah, UAE, near Mina Saqr. The projectile struck the tanker’s engine room. UKMTO said no casualties were reported and all crew members were safely evacuated. Firefighting operations were still underway when the warning was issued Thursday. India’s Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Sarbananda Sonowal, identified the vessel as the Dominica Prosperity and confirmed that 19 Indian nationals were among the 22 crew members rescued by the UAE Coast Guard. Sonowal said the tanker had been drifting off Mina Saqr when it was targeted. “The entire 22-member crew was swiftly and safely evacuated by the UAE Coast Guard and all 19 of our Indian nationals are completely safe with no injuries,” Sonowal wrote on X. He added that Indian authorities remained in contact with the vessel’s management company to coordinate support for the crew. Reuters reported that the tanker is operated by South Korea’s Sinokor Maritime Co., citing maritime risk information provider MARISKS. Maritime security company Ambrey said the vessel was struck near its stern as it exited the Strait of Hormuz. The extent of the vessel’s damage and any potential environmental impact is unknown. Multiple Tankers Struck in Separate Attacks The Dominica Prosperity incident comes amid a series of attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz. In its November 12 advisory update, the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) documented four tanker attacks since its previous report, including two in the Persian Gulf and two in the Strait of Hormuz. One of the incidents involved the tanker Fujairah Energy , which was struck by an unknown projectile while traveling eastbound in the Arabian Gulf on November 10. UKMTO said multiple crew members were injured and taken ashore for medical treatment. The remaining crew were reported safe and accounted for. No damage assessment or information about possible environmental impacts was immediately available. Another tanker, identified in the JMIC advisory as NCC Fajr, was struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on November 11. Omani authorities reported the attack at approximately 0200 UTC north of Khasab, Oman. UKMTO initially reported the incident without confirming a strike but subsequently reclassified it as an attack after receiving confirmation that the vessel had been hit. All crew members were reported safe. The fourth incident involved an unidentified tanker struck by an unknown projectile on November 10, approximately 19 nautical miles northeast of Lima, Oman, in the Strait of Hormuz. The crew was reported safe, with no environmental damage reported. The four incidents were separately documented by JMIC, although several were disclosed only after the attacks occurred. Maritime Security Threat Remains Severe JMIC said the latest attacks bring the number of recorded maritime security incidents since March 1 to 181, underscoring the continuing dangers facing commercial vessels operating in the region. JMIC attributed the continuing threat to Iranian attacks and harassment, including drone overflights, surveillance of merchant vessels and radio communications directed at ships. However, the perpetrators of the four latest projectile attacks have not been individually established in the UKMTO warnings. Commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains well below pre-conflict levels. According to JMIC, independent tracking data showed single-digit to low-double-digit vessel transits per day, while U.S. Naval Cooperation and Guidance for Shipping (NCAGS) figures indicated approximately 34 U.S.-assisted transits per day over the latest 96-hour reporting period. The two figures reflect different reporting methods and should not be treated as directly comparable measures of total traffic. The advisory also pointed to persistent congestion at anchorages near the Strait. JMIC estimated approximately 211 commercial vessels were stationary at major anchorages east of Hormuz, including Fujairah, Khor Fakkan, Sohar and Musandam. The attacks come as commercial shipping continues to navigate the dangers posed by the conflict involving Iran, the United States and Israel, with both military operations and maritime security threats complicating vessel movements through one of the world’s most important oil shipping routes. UKMTO has advised vessels operating in the region to exercise caution and report suspicious activity while authorities investigate the latest incidents. Constructed at Master Boat Builders’ shipyard in Coden, Alabama, Intrepid measures 88 feet in length and is classified as an A1 Escort Tug and Towing Vessel. articles.title: Wind-Powered Cargo Ship Neoliner Origin Cuts Fuel Consumption 70% in First Year
articles.summary: French shipping company Neoline says its wind-powered cargo vessel Neoliner Origin has delivered fuel savings of up to 70% during its first year of commercial service, offering an early test...

Join the leading maritime news network Photo Courtesy NEOLINE French shipping company Neoline says its wind-powered cargo vessel Neoliner Origin has delivered fuel savings of up to 70% during its first year of commercial service, offering an early test of whether wind propulsion can deliver substantial emissions reductions in transatlantic shipping. The 136-meter roll-on/roll-off cargo ship, which entered service in October 2025 , completed nine commercial round trips between Europe and North America, covering more than 62,000 nautical miles and carrying over 12,000 tonnes of cargo. According to first-year operating results released by Neoline, the vessel reduced fuel consumption by an average of 66% over its first year compared with conventional vessels using the Global Logistics Emissions Council (GLEC) fleet reference. Savings reached 70% when considering 2026 operations alone. The company estimates the vessel saved 3,502 tonnes of fuel over the full period, avoiding approximately 11,228 tonnes of CO2 emissions compared with the reference. The Return of Sail Power: Cargo Ships Are Turning Back to the Wind A separate analysis comparing Neoliner Origin with a simulated conventional vessel operating the same routes at 15 knots found fuel savings ranging from 62% to 67%, although Neoline acknowledged methodological uncertainty in the simulations. The results come as shipowners increasingly explore wind propulsion as a way to reduce fuel consumption and emissions without relying entirely on alternative fuels or new bunkering infrastructure. Unlike conventional cargo ships fitted with wind-assist technology, Neoliner Origin was designed from the outset to use wind as its primary means of propulsion, with its SolidSail system providing much of the power needed for transatlantic crossings. Technical Challenges Remain Despite the fuel savings, Neoline acknowledged that technical problems with the vessel’s sail system limited its performance during the first year. The company said issues affecting the sails significantly reduced the time the vessel could operate under full sail, preventing it from realizing the system’s full potential. When fully operational, however, Neoliner Origin has regularly exceeded 15 knots under sail alone. In June 2026, the vessel reached a peak speed through the water of 16.6 knots with its engine stopped. Neoline is working with French shipbuilder Chantiers de l’Atlantique to address the problems, with a maintenance period scheduled for February 2027 to restore full use of the SolidSail rig. The company is now targeting fuel savings of at least 78% against the GLEC fleet reference, with hopes of approaching or exceeding 80% during 2027. “This first year of operations confirms the potential of wind propulsion to significantly reduce fuel consumption and CO2 emissions in maritime transport,” said Jean Zanuttini, chairman and CEO of Neoline. “It has also been challenging, as can be expected when developing a prototype vessel, and has enabled us to draw valuable lessons to improve its performance.” Commercial Service Expands Beyond its environmental performance, the first year provided an opportunity to test the commercial viability of a wind-powered cargo service operating on a regular transatlantic schedule. Neoliner Origin transported 1,845 cargo units totaling approximately 12,063 tonnes and nearly 56,000 cubic meters. Cargoes included vehicles, containers, oversized industrial equipment, machinery and refrigerated goods. The vessel operates between Montoir-de-Bretagne in France and North America, with calls at Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, Baltimore and Halifax. In September, Neoline expanded the service with a new call at Zeebrugge, Belgium, providing additional access to European automotive, ro-ro and project cargo markets. Neoline also reported developing commercial partnerships with CMA CGM and CEVA, while expanding its North American relationships, including with Canadian partner Montship. The ship carried more than 170 passengers during its first year, reflecting another element of Neoline’s business model, which combines freight transportation with passenger crossings. The results offer an early indication of what wind propulsion can achieve in commercial shipping, although the vessel’s technical challenges also highlight the difficulties of bringing the technology into regular service. For Neoline, the next test will be whether improvements to the sail system can deliver more consistent performance while maintaining reliable cargo operations. “We are confident in our ability to approach, and potentially exceed, 80% fuel savings as early as 2027,” Zanuttini said. REUTERS/Yoruk Isik HELSINKI, Nov 12 (Reuters) – Finland’s military said on Thursday its forces had detected “a strike” on a Russian warship in the Baltic Sea a day earlier, but that the security situation in the area remained stable. It was not immediately clear if there were any casualties or what had caused the strike. Estonian media reported on Thursday that the vessel was a small Russian navy ship and that it later returned to St Petersburg. “The Finnish Defence Forces detected… a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland area and has monitored the development of the situation,” a spokesperson for the Nordic country’s military said in an emailed statement to Reuters. Finland is not under any immediate military threat, the spokesperson added. The defense forces declined to provide further details about the location or timing of the incident, or how it was detected. Ukraine has been sending waves of military drones towards Russia’s northwest Leningrad region, which includes the city of St Petersburg as well as the Baltic Sea port of Ust-Luga, a major export outlet for commodities such as oil and grain. Some Ukrainian drones have strayed into the airspace of Finland and the Baltic region, leading to fears that the war is spilling over into NATO countries that border Russia and its ally Belarus. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania early on Wednesday issued warnings to citizens to take shelter due to drones in their airspace, and NATO scrambled warplanes in response. The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia that extends eastwards to St Petersburg. articles.summary: Agreement combines manufacturing data and technical review to support component qualification ABS and Radian Forge have signed a joint development project (JDP) to evaluate the use of digital manufacturing data...

Join the leading maritime news network ABS and Radian Forge have signed a joint development project (JDP) to evaluate the use of digital manufacturing data in the qualification of metal components produced through wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM). As the maritime industry explores additive manufacturing to address component availability and long production lead times, confidence in the consistency and performance of manufactured parts is critical. The JDP will examine whether manufacturing process parameters, real-time sensor data, inspection records and material testing results can provide a reliable technical basis for verifying and validating WAAM-produced components. “Digital qualification has an important role to play in the adoption of additive manufacturing across the marine and offshore sectors. We are proud to work with Radian Forge to strengthen confidence in additive manufacturing by improving how qualification evidence is generated, evaluated and traced,” said Michael Kei, ABS Vice President, Technology. Under the agreement, Radian Forge will manufacture components for testing and validation, collect manufacturing and sensor data, and conduct applicable testing. ABS will provide independent technical review, evaluate test results and assess the proposed methodology and its potential application. “Traditional manufacturing timelines can create significant challenges when critical components are needed. Our goal is to build confidence in a manufacturing process that can respond to those needs. Partnering with ABS gives us an opportunity to rigorously evaluate how process data and material performance can support that objective,” said Jeff Yeager, CEO of Radian Forge. ABS supports the adoption of additive manufacturing for the maritime industry through technical requirements and guidance, including the ABS Requirements for Additive Manufacturing.
